items.stem: Which description matches a community in an ecosystem?

options.text: The populations of every species in a habitat
The individuals of one species in a habitat
The living and non-living parts of a habitat
The non-living conditions found in a habitat

items.why: A community is the populations of all the different species living together in a habitat; the ecosystem is the interaction of that community with the non-living parts of the environment.

items.stem: Which statement describes a stable community?

options.text: Population sizes stay exactly the same each year
The species stop competing for food and territory
Species and environmental factors are in balance
The abiotic factors in a habitat stay constant

items.why: A stable community is one where all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain fairly constant.

items.stem: Bacteria that live in deep sea vents are described as extremophiles. Why?

options.text: They live in water that is warmer than average
They survive by moving away from the hot water
They tolerate the extreme heat for short periods
They live in water of extreme heat and pressure

items.why: Some organisms live in environments that are very extreme, such as at high temperature, pressure, or salt concentration, and these organisms are called extremophiles; bacteria living in deep sea vents are extremophiles.

items.stem: A gardener sows seedlings very close together in fertile, well-watered soil in an open bed. Which pair of resources will these plants mainly compete for as they grow?

options.text: Light and mineral ions in the soil
Food and territory around each plant
Mates and shelter from other plants
Food and water taken up from the soil

items.why: Plants in a community or habitat often compete with each other for light and space, and for water and mineral ions from the soil, and crowded seedlings shade each other and draw on the same soil.

items.stem: A disease kills nearly all the insects that pollinate several plant species in a woodland. Which outcome best shows interdependence in this community?

options.text: Other woodland species are unaffected by this
Many other species in the wood are affected
Plants are unaffected as they feed themselves
Nothing changes as the community is stable

items.why: This is interdependence: each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc., so if one species is removed it can affect the whole community.

items.stem: Rats reach an island on a ship and begin to eat the eggs of a ground-nesting bird. Which biotic factor does this describe?

options.text: One species outcompeting another species
A new predator arriving in this community
A drop in the moisture levels of the soil
A change in the temperature of this island

items.why: New predators arriving is one of the biotic (living) factors which can affect a community, and the rats are feeding on the birds' eggs.

items.stem: Camels live in hot deserts. Which of these is a behavioural adaptation of a camel to desert conditions?

options.text: It has thick fat stored in a hump on its back
It makes small amounts of concentrated urine
It rests in the shade during the hottest hours
It has long eyelashes that keep out the sand

items.why: Adaptations may be structural, behavioural or functional, and resting in shade is something the camel does, so it is a behavioural adaptation that helps it survive in the conditions in which it normally lives.

items.stem:
The table shows the mean number of mayfly nymphs collected at four sites along one river.

Site | Dissolved oxygen in mg/dm3 | Mean number of nymphs per sample
W | 9.8 | 42
X | 8.1 | 35
Y | 5.4 | 12
Z | 3.2 | 2

Which conclusion about an abiotic factor is supported by these data?

options.text: Dissolved oxygen is a biotic factor for nymphs
Nymph numbers are constant in the whole river
Other river species are unaffected by low oxygen
Fewer nymphs were found where oxygen was lower

items.why: The data show the mean number of nymphs falling from 42 to 2 as dissolved oxygen falls from 9.8 to 3.2 mg/dm3, so this abiotic factor, oxygen levels for aquatic animals, is linked to the size of the population.

items.stem:
The table shows the numbers of a predator and of its prey counted in the same community over four years.

Year | Number of prey | Number of predators
1 | 1200 | 30
2 | 900 | 45
3 | 600 | 60
4 | 800 | 40

Which statement is best supported by these data?

options.text: Predators and prey compete for the same food
Numbers stayed constant in a stable community
Other species were unaffected by the change
Prey numbers fell as predator numbers rose

items.why: From year 1 to year 3 the prey fell from 1200 to 600 while the predators rose from 30 to 60, and in year 4 the prey rose as the predators fell, showing how a change in a biotic factor affects the community.

items.stem: How does the producer at the start of a food chain obtain its biomass?

options.text: By taking in ready-made food from soil
By feeding on other living organisms
By using photosynthesis to make glucose
By absorbing ready-made food in water

items.why: Photosynthetic organisms are the producers of biomass for life on Earth: the producer is usually a green plant or alga which makes glucose by photosynthesis.

items.stem: What is the role of microorganisms in cycling materials through an ecosystem?

options.text: They take in carbon dioxide from the air and ions from soil
They return carbon dioxide to the air and ions to the soil
They remove carbon dioxide and mineral ions from this cycle
They lock carbon dioxide and mineral ions in the dead matter

items.why: Microorganisms cycle materials by returning carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, to be used by plants in photosynthesis, and mineral ions to the soil.

items.stem: In the food chain lettuce → slug → hedgehog → fox, the hedgehog is:

options.text: a secondary consumer in the chain
a tertiary consumer in the chain
a primary consumer in the chain
a producer of biomass in the chain

items.why: Producers are eaten by primary consumers, which in turn may be eaten by secondary consumers: the hedgehog eats the slug, which is the primary consumer.

items.stem: A student places five quadrats at random in a field and counts the daisies in each: 7, 0, 6, 7, 5. What is the mean number of daisies per quadrat?

options.text: 6.0 daisies per quadrat
7.0 daisies per quadrat
5.0 daisies per quadrat
6.25 daisies per quadrat

items.why: The arithmetic mean is the total of the readings divided by the number of readings: 25 daisies divided by 5 quadrats gives 5.0 daisies per quadrat.

items.stem: Counts of daisies per quadrat range from 2 to 46. Which scale should the student use on the y-axis when plotting these results?

options.text: 0 to 50, using steps of 2, 5, 10
0 to 50, using equal steps of 5
0 to 500, using equal steps of 50
2 to 46, using steps of 4 then 10

items.why: An appropriate scale goes up in equal steps and lets the range of the data fill most of the grid, so all counts from 2 to 46 can be plotted accurately.

items.stem: Which statement describes how the water cycle provides fresh water for plants and animals on land?

options.text: Salt water drains from the seas onto the land
Water used up by organisms is lost from the land
Water is continuously evaporated and precipitated
Water is lost to the seas and is not returned

items.why: The water cycle provides fresh water for plants and animals on land before draining into the seas, because water is continuously evaporated and precipitated.

items.stem: A gardener wants rapid decay of waste plant material in a compost heap, to use the compost as a natural fertiliser. Which conditions give the fastest rate of decay?

options.text: Very hot, dry, with oxygen present
Warm, moist and with oxygen present
Warm, moist and with oxygen kept out
Warm, dry and with oxygen present

items.why: Temperature, water and the availability of oxygen affect the rate of decay, so gardeners provide optimum conditions: warm, moist and with oxygen available.

items.stem: In an investigation the mass of leaf litter in a tray fell from 60 g to 24 g in 12 days. What was the mean rate of decay?

options.text: 3.0 g per day
2.0 g per day
5.0 g per day
36.0 g per day

items.why: The rate change in decay is the change in mass divided by the time taken: 60 g minus 24 g is 36 g, and 36 g divided by 12 days is 3.0 g per day.

items.stem: Why must a biogas generator be sealed so that air cannot get in?

options.text: Methane is produced by anaerobic decay
Methane is produced faster in warmer air
Oxygen is needed to produce the methane
Bacteria need air to produce the methane

items.why: Anaerobic decay produces methane gas, so a biogas generator is sealed to keep oxygen out and produce methane gas that can be used as a fuel.

items.stem: A graph for a stable community shows that each peak in the number of lynx comes about a year after a peak in the number of hares. What does the graph show?

options.text: Predator numbers peak before prey numbers
Predator numbers peak with the prey numbers
Predator numbers stay level as prey cycle
Predator numbers peak after prey numbers

items.why: In a stable community the numbers of predators and prey rise and fall in cycles; more prey supports more predators, so the peak in predator numbers follows the peak in prey numbers.

items.stem: Thirty years ago a moss grew across a whole moor. Mean summer temperature has since risen and summer rainfall has fallen, and the moss is now found only in damp hollows. Which conclusion is best supported by this information?

options.text: Human interaction has removed it from this moor
The species is dying out across the whole moor
The plants moved downhill into the damp hollows
The availability of water limits its distribution

items.why: Environmental changes including temperature and availability of water affect the distribution of species, and the moss is now found only where water remains available.

items.stem: What is meant by the biodiversity of an ecosystem?

options.text: The total number of individual organisms there
Number of different habitats found in the area
The number of species that depend on one another
The variety of the different species living there

items.why: Biodiversity is the variety of all the different species of organisms on earth, or within an ecosystem.

items.stem: A woodland has a great biodiversity. Why is this ecosystem more stable?

options.text: The number of individual organisms stays the same
Each species depends more on others for shelter
One species depends less on others for its food
The area contains a larger number of habitats

items.why: A great biodiversity ensures the stability of ecosystems by reducing the dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment.

items.stem: As the human population grows, more untreated sewage and fertiliser drain into a river and many fish and plants die. What is the effect on the river?

options.text: There is no pollution as both are natural materials
Pollution kills organisms and biodiversity falls
Biodiversity is unchanged as fish numbers recover
Biodiversity falls but the ecosystem becomes stable

items.why: More waste is produced as the population grows, and unless it is properly handled more pollution is caused; pollution kills plants and animals which can reduce biodiversity.

items.stem: Part of an area of grassland is quarried for stone and the rest is ploughed to grow crops. What is the effect on other animals and plants?

options.text: Less land is available for other plants and animals
Quarrying reduces the land but farming does not
Biodiversity is unchanged as many individuals stay
The ecosystem is more stable once species are lost

items.why: Humans reduce the amount of land available for other animals and plants by building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste, which reduces biodiversity.

items.stem: A peat bog is drained and the peat is dug out and sold as garden compost. What are the effects?

options.text: The habitat is lost and carbon dioxide is released
Carbon dioxide is released by burning, not by decay
Biodiversity is unchanged as many organisms survive
The land stays available because it is not built on

items.why: The destruction of peat bogs to produce garden compost reduces the area of this habitat, and thus its biodiversity, and the decay or burning of the peat releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

items.stem: Levels of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere are increasing. Which is a biological consequence of the global warming this causes?

options.text: Species die out where the air becomes much warmer
Some species change the areas where they are found
Areas near carbon dioxide sources are affected most
Ecosystems become more stable as species are lost

items.why: Biological consequences of global warming include loss of habitat, changes in the distribution of species and changes in migration patterns.

items.stem: A large area of tropical forest is cleared to grow crops for biofuels. What is the impact on biodiversity?

options.text: Biodiversity is unchanged because biofuels are renewable
Biodiversity falls when the cleared trees are burned
Biodiversity falls as the forest habitat is destroyed
Biodiversity falls, so the ecosystem becomes more stable

items.why: Large-scale deforestation in tropical areas, including clearance to grow crops for biofuels, removes the habitat and so reduces the variety of species living there.

items.stem: A government wants to reduce the negative effects of humans on ecosystems and biodiversity. Which policy would have a positive impact?

options.text: Growing more crops that will be used to make biofuels
Spreading extra fertiliser on farmland each season
Digging up more peat bogs to sell as garden compost
Reducing deforestation and carbon dioxide emissions

items.why: Reduction of deforestation and of carbon dioxide emissions by some governments is one of the programmes put in place to reduce the negative effects of humans on ecosystems and biodiversity.

items.stem: Approximately what percentage of the incident energy from light do producers transfer for photosynthesis?

options.text: About 10%
About 1%
About 50%
About 90%

items.why: Producers are mostly plants and algae which transfer about 1% of the incident energy from light for photosynthesis.

items.stem: A food chain is: algae to mayfly larvae to minnow to pike. The pike has no predators in this ecosystem. Which statement about this food chain is correct?

options.text: The pike is a tertiary consumer.
The minnow is an apex predator.
The mayfly larvae are at level 1.
The pike is a secondary consumer.

items.why: The pike is a carnivore that eats another carnivore, the minnow, so it is at trophic level 4 and is called a tertiary consumer. As it has no predators it is also an apex predator.

items.stem: An oak tree of biomass 4000 kg supports 3000 caterpillars of total biomass 6 kg, which are eaten by 20 blue tits of total biomass 0.2 kg. Which description of the pyramid of biomass for these data is correct?

options.text: The oak tree is the widest bar, at the bottom.
The three bars are drawn with equal widths.
The oak tree is the narrowest bar, at the bottom.
The caterpillars form the bottom bar, as level 1.

items.why: Trophic level 1 is at the bottom of the pyramid, and the bars represent the relative amount of biomass in each level, so the oak tree with 4000 kg forms the widest bar.

items.stem: A trophic level contains 6000 g of biomass. Approximately what mass of biomass is transferred to the trophic level above it?
items.why: Only approximately 10% of the biomass from each trophic level is transferred to the level above it, and 10% of 6000 g is 600 g.

items.stem: A trophic level contains 800 g of biomass. The trophic level above it contains 40 g of biomass. What is the efficiency of the biomass transfer between these two levels?
items.why: The efficiency is the biomass transferred as a percentage of the mass available: 40 divided by 800, multiplied by 100, gives 5%.

items.stem: Which statement explains why biomass is lost between one trophic level and the next?

options.text: The uneaten parts of the prey are the main loss.
Glucose used in respiration is passed on.
Much of the glucose is used in respiration.
Producers use 10% of the light energy.

items.why: Large amounts of glucose are used in respiration, and the carbon dioxide and water produced are lost as waste, so this material is not transferred to the trophic level above.

items.stem: A food chain is: grass to rabbits to foxes. Which statement about this food chain is correct?

options.text: Similar numbers of rabbits and foxes live here.
Far fewer foxes than rabbits are supported.
More foxes than rabbits live here, as foxes hunt.
Nearly all the rabbits' biomass reaches foxes.

items.why: Only approximately 10% of the biomass from each trophic level is transferred to the level above it, so much less biomass is available to the foxes and fewer organisms can be supported at that level.

items.stem: What is meant by food security?

options.text: Growing a country's food within its borders.
Storing enough food to survive any famine.
Having enough food to feed a population.
Producing food without damaging habitats.

items.why: Food security is having enough food to feed a population, which is exactly what this option states.

items.stem: Why are some food animals fed high protein foods?

options.text: To increase their rate of growth.
To give them energy for movement.
To keep their surroundings warmer.
To reduce the food that they eat.

items.why: Some animals are fed high protein foods to increase growth, which improves the efficiency of food production.

items.stem: Mycoprotein is a protein-rich food suitable for vegetarians. How is it produced?

options.text: Bacteria are grown on glucose syrup, in aerobic conditions.
Fusarium is grown on glucose syrup, in anaerobic conditions.
Fusarium is grown on glucose syrup, in aerobic conditions.
Yeast is grown on glucose syrup, in anaerobic conditions.

items.why: The fungus Fusarium is useful for producing mycoprotein. The fungus is grown on glucose syrup, in aerobic conditions, and the biomass is harvested and purified.

items.stem: A new insect pest spreads into a country and destroys much of its wheat crop. Which biological factor affecting food security does this describe?

options.text: New pests and pathogens that affect farming.
An increasing birth rate in some countries.
Environmental change such as rains failing.
Changing diets in the developed countries.

items.why: An insect pest that has newly spread into the country and reduced the harvest is an example of new pests and pathogens that affect farming, one of the biological factors threatening food security.

items.stem: A farmer rears animals for meat indoors. Which change would improve the efficiency of food production?

options.text: Give them more space in which to move around.
Keep them in cool, well ventilated buildings.
Feed them a diet that is lower in protein.
Limit movement and control the temperature.

items.why: The efficiency of food production can be improved by restricting energy transfer from food animals to the environment, and this is done by limiting their movement and by controlling the temperature of their surroundings.

items.stem: Fish stocks in one area of ocean are declining. Which action would help to conserve the stocks at a sustainable level?

options.text: Remove quotas and keep the net size the same.
Use fishing quotas and control the net size.
Use small mesh nets to catch the young fish.
Keep fishing until the stocks begin to fall.

items.why: Control of net size and the introduction of fishing quotas play important roles in conservation of fish stocks at a sustainable level, maintaining stocks at a level where breeding continues.

items.stem: Golden rice is a genetically modified crop. How can GM crops help to meet the demands of the growing human population?

options.text: By providing medicines inside the food eaten.
By providing more food, not improved nutrition.
By providing food grown from cultured fungi.
By providing more food or improved nutrition.

items.why: GM crops could provide more food or food with an improved nutritional value such as golden rice, which is one biotechnical and agricultural solution to the demands of the growing human population.
